Title: 'Investigations on the transcendental functions which arise from the integral ∫ dx/√(1+x³)'.

(1) Definitions. Gauss sets Π(z) = ∫_{-1}^{z} dx/√(1+x³), with the lower limit at the real root of 1+x³. The inverse function is 𝔖: if Π(z)=y then z=𝔖(y). He states that 𝔖 is single-valued ('einförmig') and periodic. The sketches are the graph of 𝔖 (abscissa y, ordinate 𝔖y): over one period it is U-shaped, with minimum -1 at y=0 and poles at ±3ψ.

(2) Basic constant. ψ = Π(0) = ∫_{-1}^{0} dx/√(1+x³). Substituting x=-t gives ψ = ∫_0^1 dt/√(1-t³) = B(1/3,1/2)/3 = Γ(1/3)√π/(3Γ(5/6)) ≈ 1.4021821. The next page refines this to 1.4021822.

(3) Values and period. Gauss claims:
- 𝔖(0) = -1, 𝔖(ψ) = 0, 𝔖(2ψ) = 2, 𝔖(3ψ) = ∞;
- 𝔖 is even, 𝔖(φ) = 𝔖(-φ);
- the period is 6ψ, i.e. 𝔖(φ) = 𝔖(φ+6kψ).

Modern explanation (mine): w² = x³+1 is the equianharmonic curve, with rational torsion group Z/6:
- O (order 1), (-1,0) (order 2), (0,±1) (order 3), (2,±3) (order 6).
The real period is Ω = 2∫_{-1}^{∞} dx/√(1+x³). Measured from (-1,0) along the single real branch, the points (0,±1), (2,±3) and O lie at distances Ω/6, Ω/3 and Ω/2. Hence Ω = 6ψ and every listed value follows.

(4) Schema (x = (α+βz)/(1+δz), (1+δz)³+(α+βz)³, coefficient lists a,b,c / f,g,h, the factors 1+y and 1-y+yy). This is a search for a Möbius substitution carrying 1+x³ into a multiple of itself, i.e. one preserving dx/√(1+x³) up to sign. The result, formula 1, is x' = (2-x)/(1+x). My verification:
- (1+x)³ + (2-x)³ = 9(1-x+x²);
- hence 1+x'³ = 9(1-x+x²)/(1+x)³ and dx' = -3dx/(1+x)²;
- so dx'/√(1+x'³) = -dx/√(1+x³).
The map is an involution exchanging -1↔∞ and 0↔2. Therefore Π(x') = Π(∞) - Π(x) = 3ψ - Π(x), giving 𝔖(3ψ-φ) = (2-𝔖φ)/(1+𝔖φ). By evenness and the 6ψ period this equals 𝔖(φ+3ψ), which is Gauss's formula 1.
- In symmetric form, with m=𝔖φ and n=𝔖(3ψ∓φ): mn+m+n = 2.
- The fixed point solves x²+2x-2 = 0, so 𝔖(3ψ/2) = √3-1.

(5) Shift by 2ψ. Let s=𝔖φ and c=𝔖(φ+2ψ). Gauss gives s²c² = 4s+4c, hence c = 2(1+√(1+s³))/s². In modern terms (mine) this is translation by the 3-torsion point R=(0,1): x(P+R) = ((w-1)/s)² - s = 2(1-w)/s², with w=√(1+s³). The other root, with +w, is the other sign of R. Consistency checks:
- s=-1 gives c=2;
- s=2 gives c=-1;
- s=0 gives c∈{0,∞}.

(6) Addition theorem. From c=2(1+w)/s² one gets w = (cs²-2)/2. Gauss thus uses c to fix the sign of the square root √(1+s³). Then:
- 𝔖(3ψ+φ+φ') = [2 + ss'(s+s') - ½(cs²-2)(c's'²-2)]/(s-s')² = [2 + ss'(s+s') - 2ww']/(s-s')²;
- 𝔖(3ψ+φ-φ') is the same with +2ww'.
These are exactly the chord-tangent formulas x(P±P') = ((w∓w')/(s-s'))² - s - s' on w²=x³+1. The 3ψ appears because the base point (-1,0) sits at u=Ω/2, so P(φ)+P(φ') corresponds to parameter φ+φ'±3ψ.

The next page shifts the variable by 1 to get cleaner formulas (ß0=0, ß2φ duplication, etc.) and computes ψ by AGM-like iteration.
errors: No substantive mathematical errors found; all checked relations are correct.
Formula 1 is naturally derived as 𝔖(3ψ-φ); writing it as 𝔖(φ+3ψ) is correct only by evenness plus the 6ψ period, which Gauss has stated.
In the addition formulas the sign of ww' depends on the branch convention linking c to s (c=𝔖(φ+2ψ) versus 𝔖(φ-2ψ)). This is left implicit, but the encoding is internally consistent.

The numerical value of ψ may read 1,402186 in the image. The true value is 1.4021821, which the next page gives correctly as 1,4021822. If the last digit is indeed 6, it is a slip or a provisional value.
The schema of Möbius coefficients (a,b,c,f,g,h) is fragmentary and not carried to a stated conclusion on this page.

results.what: Inversion of ∫_{-1}^z dx/√(1+x³) to a single-valued periodic function with real period 6ψ, ψ=∫_0^1 dt/√(1-t³)
results.modern_name: Inversion of an elliptic integral; equianharmonic Weierstrass/Dixon-type elliptic function on w²=x³+1
results.usually_credited_to: Abel (1827) and Jacobi (1829) for general inversion; Gauss known privately from c.1797 (lemniscatic case)

results.what: Special values 𝔖(ψ)=0, 𝔖(2ψ)=2, 𝔖(3ψ)=∞, 𝔖(3ψ/2)=√3-1
results.modern_name: Rational torsion points (Z/6) of y²=x³+1 as division values of the period
results.usually_credited_to: Classical (division of periods: Abel; torsion of y²=x³+1 implicit in Euler/Fermat)

results.what: Möbius involution x→(2-x)/(1+x) preserving dx/√(1+x³), giving 𝔖(3ψ-φ)=(2-𝔖φ)/(1+𝔖φ)
results.modern_name: Translation by a 2-torsion point composed with negation (complement formula)
Translation by the 3-torsion point (0,1) on w²=x³+1
Addition law (chord construction) on the elliptic curve y²=x³+1
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (1750s, addition theorem for elliptic integrals)

deep.surprise_reason: Gauss's private inversion of elliptic integrals, including the lemniscatic and related equianharmonic cases, in the late 1790s is well documented. This page applies the same ideas to ∫dx/√(1+x³). It finds the 6ψ period via torsion points, a complement involution and the addition theorem, all consistent with known Gauss material and with Euler's addition theorem. It is a nice explicit unpublished worked case, but not a new attribution.
